title: The odd nights
hookLine: seek the Night of Power in the odd nights of the last ten (Bukhari)

cards: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ steps out of his house with news. He knows which night it is, the Night of Power, and he's coming to tell the people. But outside, two men are arguing.

By the time the quarrel is done, the knowledge has been lifted from him. The report, from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, is in Sahih al-Bukhari, and what the Prophet says next is the surprise. Perhaps it's better for you this way.

teach.b: First, the night itself. The Qur'an gives it a short surah of its own, the ninety-seventh. In Pickthall's words: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months."
The surah opens by saying the Qur'an was sent down on that night, and the hadith place it in Ramadan. Second, where to look.

teach.h: THE ODD NIGHTS OF THE LAST TEN.
teach.b: In another report in Bukhari, the Prophet says to seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan. Not one night, then: a handful near the end of the month, each one a candidate. Third, why not just say which?
The story of the quarrel answers that, at least in part. The date was about to be given and was taken away, and the Prophet didn't call it a loss.
If the date were known, people might pour everything into one night and coast through the rest. Unknown, it asks for attention across several nights, and it rewards the person who keeps showing up.
Some scholars have drawn that lesson; the hadith itself leaves the reason unsaid. Fourth, what people do.
Aisha describes the Prophet, when the last ten began, tightening his waist-wrapper, staying up through the night, and waking his family.
In some mosques the last ten nights are full: long prayers, recitation, some people staying in the mosque altogether, children asleep on the carpets at the back.
Others keep the odd nights at home, quietly.
Either way, the search is the practice. And one small detail from that first story: what hid the night was two men arguing. A quarrel can cost more than the people in it.

how: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, Muslims who keep them spend extra hours in prayer and recitation, especially on the odd nights; some stay in the mosque for the whole ten days, and others keep the nights at home.

games.q: you've come out to tell the people which night is the Night of Power. two men are arguing, and the knowledge is taken from you. what do you say?
o: perhaps it is better for you; seek it.
games.why: perhaps it is better for you. the night isn't lost, just hidden, and the people are told to seek it.

practice: If you pray, choose one night this week, or mark the odd nights of the next Ramadan, and plan a few extra minutes of prayer or recitation before you sleep.
If you don't, sit with the idea of a night worth staying up for, and ask what you'd want to have done with it. No grand plan: one night, a little longer awake.
